To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
“African dust input to the NW African Atlantic margin is controlled by the precession of Earth’s axis of rotation, which is a consequence of its obliquity.

“Precessional forcing of terrigenous supply from Northwest Africa to North Atlantic during the last ∼220 kyr is recognized through changes in physical (sediment colour and magnetic susceptibility) and geochemical (XRF element intensity) sediment properties.

(1) precession forcing of dust flux to the North Atlantic is recognised through changes of sediment properties in a core from NW Africa; (2) precessional maxima in terrigenous supply coincide with precession minima; (3) this suggests a close link to monsoon activity; (4) enhanced precession-driven solar insolation would have caused increased temperature contrasts, which stimulated storminess.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a better understanding of the relationship between precession and dust flux, and how it is modulated by storminess.
the control that precession has over dust input to the North Atlantic Ocean and the implications for the dust source region.
a possible link between precession-driven changes in summer insolation and African dust input to Northwest Africa during the last 200 kyr.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
precession is the major control of African dust input into the Moroccan Atlantic margin.
dust input to the Atlantic from the NW African continent during the last 2.2 Myr was controlled by precessional forcing.
precessional forcing of the North African monsoon system is responsible for the observed changes in dust flux to the North Atlantic Ocean.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the precession signal of the last 250 kyr is clearly recorded in our core, but only in the dust-related proxies.
the dust input from North African deserts to the North Atlantic Ocean was controlled by precessional changes in the strength and frequency of summer storms.
precessional control over dust flux from Northwest African to the Atlantic during glacial–interglacial periods is mainly driven by changes in summer insolation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dust flux from the Sahara to the adjacent Atlantic Ocean was modulated by the precession of the Earth’s axis of rotation.
precession-driven solar forcing has a major control over dust generation in the Sahara and its subsequent transport to the adjacent North African Atlantic margin.
dust fluxes to the North Atlantic are not controlled by the monsoon system alone.
